core_idea: A way is a route or a direction that something goes, or the manner in which something is done.

senses.definition: a method or manner of doing something

examples.text: What is the best way to learn a language?
There are several ways of cooking rice.
I like the way you have arranged the room.
Do it this way, not that way.

items: there is no way of knowing

subsenses.definition: the manner in which a person usually acts, as part of their character

examples.text: Don't mind him; it's just his way.
Grandfather is set in his ways and hates any change.

adaptation.grammar: The way is followed directly by a clause: the way she talks, the way it works. Do not add how; that or in which is possible but rare in speech.

senses.definition: the route or path that leads to a place, or that you take to get there

examples.text: Can you tell me the way to the station?
We lost our way in the dark.
Is this the way to the beach?
The way in is around the back of the building.

compare.note: a road is the thing built; a way is the route you take

subsenses.definition: the route that someone makes or follows, used after a verb that says how they move

examples.text: She pushed her way through the crowd.
We felt our way along the dark hall.
The river winds its way down to the sea.
He worked his way to the top of the company.

senses.definition: the direction in which someone or something goes, faces, or points

examples.text: Which way did they go?
Look this way and smile!
Turn the key the other way.
The sign is facing the wrong way.

senses.definition: the distance between two points, or the length of time until something happens

examples.text: The hotel is a long way from the beach.
We still have a long way to go before the work is finished.
The shop is only a little way down the road.
Summer is still a long way off.

senses.definition: the space that someone or something needs in order to move or pass

examples.text: A fallen tree blocked the way.
Please move your bike; it's in the way.
The police cleared the way for the ambulance.

senses.definition: one particular side of a matter or a situation, seen on its own

examples.text: In many ways, the new job is better than the old one.
The two brothers are alike in every way.
The plan worked in one way but failed in another.
In some ways I'm glad we moved.

senses.definition: the area where someone lives, works, or happens to be

examples.text: Come and see us if you're ever out our way.
They live somewhere over your way, I think.
Nothing much happens down our way.

phrases.definition: used to add something that is not connected with what you were saying, or that you have just remembered
phrases.explanation: Speakers often use by the way to bring up the thing they most wanted to say, as if it were unimportant.

examples.text: By the way, did you call your mother?
I saw Lee yesterday, by the way; he sends his love.

phrases.definition: partly, or from one point of view
phrases.explanation: Also in some ways, in one way, and in many ways. In no way means not at all.

examples.text: In a way, I'm glad the trip was cancelled.
He's right, in a way, but it isn't the whole story.

phrases.definition: certainly not
phrases.explanation: Used to refuse or to show that you do not believe something. There's no way (that) something will happen means it is impossible.

examples.text: Lend you my car? No way!
No way is she only thirty!
There's no way we can get there by six.

phrases.definition: while going from one place to another
phrases.explanation: Someone who is on the way, or on their way, is coming; a baby that is on the way has not been born yet. Something that is on the way out is going out of fashion.

examples.text: I'll pick up some bread on the way home.
Sara called to say she's on her way.
They have a second baby on the way.

phrases.definition: break or fall down because of the weight or force on it
phrases.explanation: Give way to something means be replaced by it, or agree to it after refusing. In British English drivers give way to other traffic, which Americans call yield.

examples.text: The old bridge gave way under the weight of the truck.
Her anger slowly gave way to tears.
examples.note: give way to: be replaced by

examples.text: In the end, he gave way and let the children stay up late.

phrases.definition: be in a position or a situation that stops someone from moving, seeing, or doing something
phrases.explanation: Get in the way of something means stop it from happening or from being done well.

examples.text: Move those boxes; they're getting in the way.
Don't let your pride get in the way of an apology.

phrases.definition: in a position that stops someone from passing, seeing, or doing something

examples.text: Am I in your way?
A large truck was parked right in the way.

phrases.definition: no longer in a position where you block someone, or in a place far from towns and people
phrases.explanation: Get something out of the way means finish it so that you need not think about it any more. An out-of-the-way place is far from anywhere.

examples.text: Get out of the way, the bus is coming!
Let's get the boring jobs out of the way first.
examples.note: finished and no longer a worry

examples.text: They live in a small village, a little out of the way.

phrases.definition: the opposite of what has just been said or of what you might expect
phrases.explanation: Also means in the opposite order or position. British English also says the other way round.

examples.text: I don't work for him; it's the other way around, he works for me.
You've put the batteries in the other way around.

phrases.definition: the typical way that a person or a group lives, with its habits, work, and beliefs

examples.text: Fishing has been a way of life in the village for hundreds of years.
Moving to the city meant a whole new way of life.

phrases.definition: the whole distance to a place, or completely and to the end
phrases.explanation: Go all the way can also mean, informally, have sex.

examples.text: We walked all the way to the top of the hill.
She was with me all the way through the illness.
If you start, you must go all the way.

phrases.definition: through a place, as a route, or as a kind of something

examples.text: They flew to the island by way of the capital.
He said a few words by way of introduction.

phrases.definition: move to one side so that someone or something can pass
phrases.explanation: Make way for something also means be replaced by it.

examples.text: Make way, please! Let the nurse through.
The old cinema was pulled down to make way for apartments.
examples.note: make way for: be replaced by

phrases.definition: go somewhere, especially slowly or with difficulty
phrases.explanation: Make your way in the world means become successful by your own efforts.

examples.text: We made our way slowly through the crowd.
The guests made their way to the dining room.

phrases.definition: make a special effort to do something, more than is expected of you

examples.text: The hotel staff went out of their way to make us comfortable.
Don't go out of your way to get it; I can wait.

phrases.definition: no matter which of two things happens, is true, or is chosen

examples.text: We can eat in or go out; either way is fine with me.
Either way, we need to leave by eight.

phrases.definition: by some method, even if you do not yet know which
phrases.explanation: Also means for one reason or another, or in one of several possible ways. One way or the other is used in the same way.

examples.text: One way or another, we'll get the money.
Everyone was affected by the storm, one way or another.

phrases.definition: make other people let you do what you want
phrases.explanation: Also have your own way. Have it your way is said, often with annoyance, when you stop arguing and let someone do as they want.

examples.text: Kim always gets her own way in the end.
Fine, have it your way; we'll take the bus.
examples.note: have it your way, said with annoyance

phrases.definition: end a relationship or a period together and live or work apart

examples.text: After college, the two friends went their separate ways.

phrases.definition: by having a bad experience, rather than by being told or taught
phrases.explanation: Used with learn, find out, and do.

examples.text: I learned the hard way that you should always keep a copy of your files.
Some people have to find things out the hard way.

phrases.definition: used to praise someone who has just done something well

examples.text: You passed! Way to go, Ravi!
Way to go, Sam, you've broken the printer again.

phrases.definition: have a natural ability to deal well with something or someone
phrases.explanation: Have a way with words means speak or write well; have a way with children or animals means handle them well.

examples.text: Omar has a way with words.
She has a way with difficult customers.

phrases.definition: go first to show the route, or be the first to do something new

examples.text: You know the building, so you lead the way.
The company led the way in making cheaper phones.

phrases.definition: make it possible or easier for something to happen later

examples.text: The new law paved the way for cleaner factories.

phrases.definition: very much, or on a large scale

examples.text: The town has changed in a big way since the factory came.

phrases.definition: of the kind mentioned
phrases.explanation: Used mostly after not much, nothing, or what.

examples.text: There isn't much in the way of entertainment in the village.
What do you have in the way of vegetarian food?

phrases.definition: be very useful or effective, or last for a long time
phrases.explanation: Go a long way toward doing something means help a lot.

examples.text: A little politeness goes a long way.
The money won't go a long way with prices like these.

phrases.definition: make a lot of progress

examples.text: Your English has come a long way since last year.
The town has come a long way since the mine closed.

phrases.definition: make someone a little angry without meaning to, by the way you act
phrases.explanation: The British form is rub someone up the wrong way.

examples.text: Something about his tone rubbed her the wrong way.

phrases.definition: used to say that something is certainly true, even if it is unwelcome

examples.text: We're lost, no two ways about it.

phrases.text: laugh all the way to the bank
phrases.definition: make a lot of money easily, especially from something that others thought foolish

examples.text: The critics hated the film, but the studio laughed all the way to the bank.

phrases.definition: very ill, or in serious trouble

examples.text: After the fall, the old dog was in a bad way.
The company is in a bad way and may close.

phrases.definition: choose not to notice something wrong that you could stop

examples.text: The guards looked the other way while the goods were carried out.

phrases.definition: be familiar with a place or a subject, so that you can deal with it easily

examples.text: She knows her way around the kitchen.
Ask Lee; he knows his way around the tax rules.

phrases.definition: a method of escaping from a difficult situation

examples.text: There seemed to be no way out of the debt.
Selling the car gave them a way out.

phrases.definition: the best action to take next

examples.text: Talking to each other is the only way forward.

word_family.note: informal: by a large amount, as in way too big

synonym_discrimination.note: Way is the everyday word for how something is done: the best way to cook rice. A method is a way that is planned and can be described step by step, often in work or science: a new teaching method. Manner is more formal and is used mostly for the way a person behaves or speaks: in a polite manner. Means is the thing you use to reach a result: a means of transport, a means of earning money.

usage_note: The way is followed directly by a clause: the way she sings, not the way how she sings. That is possible after the way (the way that it works) but is usually left out. Way is also an informal adverb, mostly American, meaning by a large amount: way too big, way behind; that use has its own entry.

learner_errors.incorrect: I like the way how she talks.
learner_errors.correct: I like the way she talks.
learner_errors.note: A clause follows the way directly; how is never added.

learner_errors.incorrect: Sorry, am I on your way?
learner_errors.correct: Sorry, am I in your way?
learner_errors.note: In the way means blocking someone; on the way means during a journey.

learner_errors.incorrect: We stopped at the shop by the way home.
learner_errors.correct: We stopped at the shop on the way home.
learner_errors.note: By the way changes the subject; on the way means during the journey.

adaptation.semantic: Way covers a route, a direction, a manner, a distance, and a respect (in some ways), which most languages divide among several words; translate by sense. The fixed phrases by the way (changing the subject), in a way (partly), and no way (certainly not) cannot be translated word for word.
adaptation.grammar: Way is countable: a way, two ways, a way of doing something, the way to do it. A clause follows directly: the way she talks, with no how. After a verb of movement a possessive is used: pushed his way, worked her way up.
adaptation.pronunciation: Rhymes with day and say: the letters ay stand for the vowel of face. Ways ends with a z sound.
